title: Heliofin x Redwood Inference — Procurement / Legal Redlines (Security Appendix + SOC 2 NDA)
summary: Heliofin procurement/legal walked through redlines to Redwood’s Security Appendix and the evidence request list. Main topics: (1) SOC 2 Type II report access under NDA and what Redwood can share pre-NDA (SOC 2 cover letter/bridge letter + high-level controls summary), (2) incident notification language (commitments must remain contract-dependent and avoid “immediate/within X hours” unless negotiated), (3) data retention and deletion wording (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private responsibilities), and (4) audit log scope and export (what’s in product today vs roadmap). Redwood agreed to route Security Appendix redlines through Legal + GRC, and to provide Heliofin with the standard NDA template and evidence request process/timeline.

SOC 2 Type II report access: NDA requirement and distribution tracking
Incident response and notification language constraints
Data retention, deletion requests, and shared responsibility by deployment mode
Audit logging scope, SIEM export, and evidence pointers

Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Heliofin x Redwood Inference — Procurement / Legal Redlines (Security Appendix + SOC 2 NDA)
Recorded: 2026-02-12 17:00:14 UTC
Duration: 38 min

Attendees
- Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood) — Account Executive
- Markus Klein (Redwood) — Solutions Engineering
- Olga Petrov (Redwood) — GRC / Compliance
- Sofia Mendes (Redwood) — Commercial Counsel
- Priya Desai (Heliofin) — Procurement Lead
- Tom Gallagher (Heliofin) — Senior Counsel
- Mina Park (Heliofin) — Security Program Manager
- Alex Chen (Heliofin) — IT Director


Summary (auto-generated)
Heliofin requested SOC 2 report access and clarified NDA requirements. Parties reviewed Security Appendix redlines, focusing on incident notification, data retention, audit logs, and evidence sharing process. Redwood confirmed it can share some high-level materials pre-NDA and will share the SOC 2 report only after NDA execution, with controlled distribution.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) NDA + SOC 2 access
2) Security Appendix redlines workflow
3) Incident notification language
4) Retention/deletion and logging scope

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send NDA template and evidence request process
- Heliofin to send consolidated markup of appendix
- Redwood Legal/GRC to return redlines response


Transcript

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright, I think we’re good. Thanks everyone for making the time. This is Stephanie from Redwood. We also have Markus, Olga from our GRC team, and Sofia from legal.

[00:10] Priya Desai: Hi, Priya here. Thanks. We’ve got Tom from legal, Mina from security, and Alex from IT. Goal today is basically close out the last set of redlines on the security appendix and figure out what we need for SOC 2 and… the evidence list.

[00:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. That matches what I have. And just to level set, we’re not trying to negotiate the full MSA on this call, but we can walk through the appendix language and our evidence sharing process.

[00:40] Tom Gallagher: Yeah, understood. We’re focusing on the security addendum / appendix language that got attached to the order form. There are like… three key issues and then a few smaller ones.

[00:50] Mina Park: And on my side it’s mostly SOC 2 scope, pen test summary, and clarity on what your audit logs actually contain.

[01:00] Markus Klein: Great. Happy to cover audit logs and what’s in-product today.

[01:06] Sofia Mendes: And I can cover the redline workflow and what we can and can’t accept as written.

[01:12] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Priya, do you want to start with SOC 2 and NDA? That seems to be gating a bunch.

[01:19] Priya Desai: Yes. So, we requested the SOC 2 Type II report. Our policy is we can sign an NDA for that. But we need the report to move forward. Can you share it without the NDA? Or at least a portion?

[01:34] Olga Petrov: I can take that. We require an NDA before sharing the full SOC 2 Type II report. That’s standard for us. What we can share pre-NDA is typically a SOC 2 cover letter and, depending on the request, a high-level controls summary. But the full report with testing detail is NDA only.

[01:55] Tom Gallagher: Is that negotiable? Some vendors just provide it.

[02:00] Olga Petrov: For the full report, generally no. We also track distribution—who receives the report, version, date—because it contains sensitive details about our controls and exceptions. Once the NDA is in place, turnaround is usually within one to two business days.

[02:18] Mina Park: When you say “cover letter,” do you mean like the opinion letter from the auditor? Or a bridge letter?

[02:25] Olga Petrov: Bridge letter, yes—like a period-of-time statement if needed, plus an attestation cover. I don’t want to over-promise the exact format on this call, but we can share what we have in our standard package.

[02:40] Alex Chen: And just to confirm, this is SOC 2 Type II for the hosted service? Or does it cover your dedicated and private deployments too?

[02:48] Olga Petrov: The SOC 2 report covers Redwood’s controls for the platform services under the audited scope. For Dedicated and Private, the shared responsibility boundary shifts. The report itself doesn’t magically “cover” your environment—especially for Private where it’s customer-managed networking and potentially customer-managed infra. But our organizational controls still apply for what we operate.

[03:10] Markus Klein: Yeah, and for Private, we’re usually very explicit: Redwood provides the control plane and deployment artifacts, and you control the underlying environment depending on VPC/on-prem. So the evidence we share will map to what we do vs what you do.

[03:26] Mina Park: That’s fine. We’re likely doing Dedicated, not fully on-prem. But we need clarity in the appendix language, because some of it reads like you’re responsible for everything end-to-end.

[03:36] Sofia Mendes: Right, and we typically won’t accept language that implies we are responsible for customer-controlled environment elements. We can propose alternative wording that aligns to shared responsibility.

[03:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. So next step on SOC 2: we’ll send the NDA template right after this call. Priya, do you have a preferred process—like do you want us to countersign, or do you have your own NDA?

[03:58] Priya Desai: We can start with yours, it’s faster. We do have our own but it takes longer.

[04:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[04:07] Tom Gallagher: On the NDA, we need it to allow sharing with our auditors as well. Sometimes vendors restrict it to internal only.

[04:15] Sofia Mendes: That’s a good flag. Our standard NDA allows sharing with advisors under confidentiality obligations, but I need to verify the exact clause. If we need a tweak, we can do that. It’s usually straightforward.

[04:30] Priya Desai: Okay.

[04:32] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Let’s shift to the security appendix redlines. Tom, do you want to walk us through the must-haves?

[04:39] Tom Gallagher: Yep. The first is incident notification. Our template says you notify us “without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours” of any security incident impacting our data. Your version is more… flexible.

[04:55] Sofia Mendes: Correct, our language is intentionally not a fixed hour commitment unless it’s negotiated as part of a specific SLA or security addendum. We commit to notification consistent with the agreement and applicable law, and we avoid “within X hours” as a blanket statement.

[05:12] Mina Park: But from a security standpoint, 24 hours is pretty standard.

[05:16] Olga Petrov: It’s common, but we need to align it to the incident definition and investigation reality. There are cases where we may have indicators but not confirmed impact yet. We don’t want to notify prematurely with wrong information. We do commit to timely communication, but the exact timeline is typically contract-dependent.

[05:37] Tom Gallagher: Our concern is if it’s “reasonable efforts” it can stretch.

[05:41] Sofia Mendes: Understood. We can propose a compromise that’s more specific without being absolute. For example, notification “without undue delay after confirmation of unauthorized access to Customer Data” or similar. But I’m not committing to that exact sentence live.

[06:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Right, we’ll capture it as an action item: Sofia will come back with alternative language we can approve.

[06:07] Tom Gallagher: Okay. Second, there’s a clause about audit rights. Our template asks for the right to conduct on-site audits and penetration tests.

[06:16] Sofia Mendes: Yeah, we generally don’t allow on-site audits of our facilities or systems by individual customers. We provide third-party audit reports (SOC 2) and may provide additional evidence under NDA. For pen tests, we do them, but we don’t allow customers to pen test our multi-tenant hosted production environment.

[06:35] Alex Chen: Even on Dedicated?

[06:38] Markus Klein: Dedicated is dedicated capacity, but it still sits within our managed environment. We can talk about customer testing in a controlled manner, but it’s not a blanket “go run scans” permission.

[06:50] Mina Park: We mainly want assurance we can validate controls.

[06:54] Olga Petrov: And that’s where the evidence package comes in: SOC 2, pen test executive summary, vulnerability management overview, and so on. We can also do targeted security review sessions.

[07:08] Priya Desai: Our procurement team will accept SOC 2 in lieu of audits for most vendors, but legal wants the clause.

[07:14] Sofia Mendes: We can propose standard language: no customer on-site audit, but we provide independent audit reports and respond to reasonable questionnaires. That’s typical.

[07:26] Tom Gallagher: Third item is data retention and deletion. Your appendix says “we retain logs for up to 30 days” and our security team wants it spelled out: prompt and completion data, telemetry, audit logs—how long, can we request deletion, what’s the default.

[07:44] Markus Klein: Just to separate: audit logs are different from inference payload logs.

[07:48] Mina Park: Right, and your FAQ we saw was a little vague.

[07:52] Stephanie Nguyen: We have updated one-pagers on retention and residency that should be more specific. Markus can send those.

[07:59] Olga Petrov: On retention, we avoid hard “always” statements because it can differ by deployment mode and by configuration. Hosted has certain defaults. Dedicated can have more configurable retention depending on setup. Private is often customer-controlled for certain log layers.

[08:17] Alex Chen: Can you just say you don’t train on our data? That’s another question.

[08:21] Markus Klein: Yes, for our platform, by default we don’t use customer prompts and outputs to train our base models. But we should provide the approved wording in the FAQ; Stephanie can send it in the package.

[08:33] Sofia Mendes: We need to be careful on phrasing. We can say we do not use Customer Content to train models without customer authorization, consistent with our terms. I’ll defer to the approved language.

[08:46] Mina Park: The retention question for us is: if we’re in Hosted, can we set retention to zero? Like no payload logging.

[08:54] Markus Klein: In Hosted, we have operational logging for reliability and abuse prevention. Some payload logging can be minimized, and there are options for redaction and retention limits. I don’t want to misstate; the retention controls one-pager outlines what is configurable today.

[09:14] Olga Petrov: And deletion requests: we have a process to handle customer deletion requests, but again, it depends on what data category and whether it’s in backups or logs. We usually state we’ll comply within a reasonable timeframe and per contract.

[09:28] Tom Gallagher: Our template is strict: delete within 30 days and certify deletion.

[09:33] Sofia Mendes: Certification is tricky because of backups and immutable logs. We can propose an alternative: deletion of active systems and expiration from backups on a defined schedule, but not immediate purge from all backups. Pretty standard.

[09:50] Priya Desai: Okay, we’ll need your counterproposal there too.

[09:55] Stephanie Nguyen: Got it.

[10:00] Mina Park: Can we talk about evidence sharing? We asked for SOC 2, pen test, vuln scan results, subprocessor list, and a copy of your incident response plan.

[10:12] Olga Petrov: Yes. So the evidence sharing process is: once NDA is executed, we can share SOC 2 Type II report. For pen tests, we typically share an executive summary under NDA, not the full detailed findings. For subprocessors, we can share the list; some of that is also publicly available depending on the item.

[10:30] Mina Park: And the incident response plan?

[10:32] Olga Petrov: We do not share the full internal incident response playbook. We can share a customer-facing incident response and notification overview—the one-pager—describing how we detect, triage, and communicate, without disclosing sensitive internal procedures.

[10:49] Alex Chen: That’s common.

[10:51] Tom Gallagher: What about policies? Like access control policy.

[10:54] Olga Petrov: Again, we generally don’t share internal policy documents in full. SOC 2 provides independent validation of the controls. We can answer questionnaires and provide summaries.

[11:07] Priya Desai: Okay. For procurement, we mainly need SOC 2 and confirmation of insurance and subprocessors.

[11:14] Stephanie Nguyen: Insurance is separate but I can get you the certificate through the right channel.

[11:19] Sofia Mendes: One more point: for evidence, we need to keep the distribution limited to named recipients. So when you sign the NDA, we’ll ask who will receive the SOC 2 report.

[11:30] Mina Park: That’s okay. We can give you names.

[11:33] Markus Klein: Mina, on audit logs specifically, what is your requirement? Like do you need SIEM export? What events?

[11:40] Mina Park: Yeah. We need admin action logs: who created API keys, changed roles, SSO configuration changes, model access, that sort of thing. And we need export to Splunk.

[11:54] Markus Klein: Okay, so Redwood Console has audit events for admin actions—things like API key creation, key rotation, user/role changes, SSO settings updates. Export: today we support download and streaming to certain endpoints; for Splunk specifically it’s usually via a generic webhook or S3 delivery that Splunk can ingest. I need to double-check the current integration wording so we don’t misstate.

[12:20] Alex Chen: Is it real-time?

[12:22] Markus Klein: Near real-time, but I don’t want to promise a specific latency. It’s not like milliseconds.

[12:30] Mina Park: Okay. Also, do you log prompts? Like do audit logs contain content?

[12:35] Markus Klein: Audit logs are about control plane actions, not prompt content. Content logging is a separate category and is governed by retention settings and operational requirements.

[12:48] Olga Petrov: And we can provide the audit logging overview one-pager that separates those categories.

[12:55] Tom Gallagher: In the appendix, there’s a line that says “Vendor maintains audit logs for all access to Customer Data.” That’s what we inserted. Is that accurate?

[13:05] Markus Klein: That’s… probably too broad as written. We can log administrative access, but “all access to customer data” is not a statement we’d want to sign without defining what counts as access and what systems. For example, runtime systems handling inference requests—there is operational telemetry, but not necessarily a per-access audit trail like a database.

[13:29] Sofia Mendes: Exactly. That’s the kind of overbroad statement we’ll counter-redline. We need to scope audit logging to what we actually log.

[13:38] Tom Gallagher: Understood, but we need something.

[13:41] Olga Petrov: We can propose language that we maintain audit logs for administrative access to production systems and for control plane actions, and we can provide those logs to you upon request or via export features, depending on product tier.

[13:58] Mina Park: That would likely pass.

[14:01] Priya Desai: Can we talk about timing? We’re trying to close this by end of month.

[14:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. If we get consolidated redlines by tomorrow or Saturday, we can turn a response early next week. NDA we can do tomorrow.

[14:16] Tom Gallagher: I already sent redlines in email.

[14:19] Stephanie Nguyen: We saw those, but there were two versions—one from legal and one from security. If you can consolidate into one markup with a priority list, that helps us respond faster.

[14:31] Tom Gallagher: Fair.

[14:33] Mina Park: Another question—subprocessors. Is the list up to date? And do you notify us of changes?

[14:40] Olga Petrov: We maintain a subprocessor list and a notification process. We can share the list and the notification method (typically email notice with a notice period). The exact notice period can be in the DPA.

[14:56] Sofia Mendes: And we generally include subprocessor notice and objection process in the DPA rather than the security appendix. If you’re asking for DPA updates, we should keep those in the right document.

[15:08] Tom Gallagher: We’ll check. We may need the DPA anyway because of data processing.

[15:12] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s normal. We can route DPA via our legal process.

[15:17] Alex Chen: Is data residency relevant? We’re mostly US, but we have EU clients.

[15:22] Markus Klein: Residency depends on deployment. Hosted has specific regions. Dedicated can be in region, with isolation. Private can be in your VPC in-region. We have a data residency one-pager that lists region availability and what metadata might still flow for ops.

[15:44] Mina Park: Our key concern is whether telemetry or logs leave the region.

[15:47] Olga Petrov: We can explain it precisely: some operational metrics may be centralized depending on configuration, but we avoid moving customer content across regions without reason. Again, the one-pager covers defaults and configuration options, and we’re careful not to claim “never.”

[16:07] Tom Gallagher: Okay.

[16:09] Priya Desai: Can you send that one-pager now, so we can align internally?

[16:12] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, we’ll send the whole updated security kit—FAQ and the one-pagers.

[16:18] Markus Klein: I’ll send audit logging and retention one-pagers specifically.

[16:23] Priya Desai: Great.

[16:25] (crosstalk)

[16:26] Speaker 1: Sorry—on incident notice, we want to ensure it includes “suspected incident,” not just confirmed.

[16:33] Sofia Mendes: That’s a common request. The problem is it can create noise. We can maybe commit to notifying upon confirmation of a security incident affecting your data, and separately provide status updates as more info is available. We can also include a commitment to keep you informed during investigation.

[16:55] Mina Park: If it’s suspected and then later you find out it’s real, we don’t want to be days behind.

[17:01] Olga Petrov: Totally. Practically, we often communicate early, but contract language needs a workable trigger. We can propose something like “promptly” after determination that Customer Data is impacted, with an obligation to notify if we reasonably believe there was unauthorized access. Again, we’ll come back with approved language.

[17:27] Tom Gallagher: Okay.

[17:29] Alex Chen: Do you have a status page? For incidents.

[17:32] Markus Klein: Yes, Redwood has a status page. We can provide the link, and it’s also referenced in the incident response one-pager.

[17:40] Mina Park: Great.

[17:42] Stephanie Nguyen: Anything else we should cover before we recap?

[17:46] Priya Desai: One more procurement item: we need a single email with “what we’re getting” for evidence: SOC 2, pen test summary, subprocessor list, retention statement. Our internal tracker is messy.

[17:58] Stephanie Nguyen: Yep. I can send a single package email with links/attachments and note what’s NDA-gated.

[18:06] Tom Gallagher: Also, please confirm that the SOC 2 is the latest period. Some vendors provide outdated.

[18:12] Olga Petrov: We’ll confirm the period covered. If there’s a gap, we can include a bridge letter.

[18:20] Mina Park: For pen test, we’re okay with an executive summary if it includes scope and remediation status.

[18:26] Olga Petrov: That’s typically what it includes.

[18:30] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. Let’s do recap.

[18:33] Stephanie Nguyen: Redwood to send NDA template today/tomorrow morning. Once executed, Olga will share SOC 2 Type II report and the pen test executive summary under NDA, plus subprocessor list. Markus will send audit logging and retention one-pagers and clarify the SIEM export capabilities without roadmap commitments. Tom will send consolidated appendix redlines with priority list. Sofia will review and come back with approved counter-language, especially for incident notification, audit rights, and deletion/certification clauses. Does that capture it?

[19:10] Priya Desai: Yes.

[19:11] Tom Gallagher: Works.

[19:12] Mina Park: Yep.

[19:13] Alex Chen: Sounds good.

[19:16] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Thanks all — we’ll aim to turn redlines early next week.

[19:22] Call ended.
